paragraphs.source_en: Outside Edo Castle's Asakusa Gate, on the bank of the Sumida River, stood the imposing residence of Matsudaira Tadateru. Ōkubo Nagayasu had chosen the site and built the residence, which was now more than three times its original size.

units.source_en: Outside Edo Castle's Asakusa Gate, on the bank of the Sumida River, stood the imposing residence of Matsudaira Tadateru.

units.source_zh: 此府邸原为大久保长安择地而建，如今比刚建成时的规模已增了三倍还多。

paragraphs.source_en: Within the Asakusa Gate, only a cramped parcel could have been allotted; moreover, this site bordered the Sumida, where boats carrying the annual tribute of the Eight Provinces of Kantō gathered, so the other daimyō were deeply envious and greatly admired Nagayasu's discernment.

paragraphs.source_en: Nagayasu had lately been impossibly busy. He had gone first from the mines of Iwami to Nara, then to Tadateru's domain in Shinano to supervise embankment construction, and afterward had traveled from his own residence in Hachiōji to Edo. Only upon reaching Edo did he learn that Ieyasu had returned from Fushimi. He therefore decided to proceed to Sado only after preparing the marriage of Tadateru and Date Masamune's eldest daughter.

paragraphs.source_en: Two days after Nagayasu reached the residence, a procession followed him there: women whom he intended to take to Sado. Their splendid Kyoto-style dress astonished the people of Edo. At first people took them for attendants of Tadateru's bride, but when they realized that the women had come from the opposite direction to Ōshū, some began saying they were kabuki performers recruited in Kyoto.
